XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move the amendment tabled in my name. As Members are already aware, I am living with prostate cancer and, as such, I believe that that experience has given me a real insight into the challenges faced by patients and indeed their families across Wales. As has already been said, I'm one of more than 2,500 men who are diagnosed with prostate cancer every year here in Wales and, as we've already heard, around 640 men die from it.

It's because of the high prevalence of men in Wales who are diagnosed with it that I believe it has to be included in the national cancer strategy for Wales. Indeed, in the written questions that I've tabled to the Cabinet Minister, the responses have included actions that would be taken via the national cancer strategy, and so I have no reason to believe that it wouldn't inform some part of the future thinking of this Government.

I have to say that I welcome the consultation on the national cancer strategy, because it's a good opportunity to think a bit more innovatively about how services can be delivered in the future. However, this consultation must be more than a tick-box exercise, and as we've so often heard in the past, whether it's a Welsh Government consultation or a health board consultation, patients' voices must be heard. It's absolutely essential that this consultation is meaningful, that those who engage with it are confident that their views are genuinely being considered, and that the final strategy reflects the submissions it receives. So, I hope that the Cabinet Minister will give that assurance to us today in his response to this debate.

Now, as our amendment makes very clear, the Welsh Conservatives want to see a national screening programme introduced by the Welsh Government. I believe that earlier detection improves patient outcomes, and as Prostate Cancer Research tells us, when prostate cancer is detected early, survival rates are close to 100 per cent. And this is not a party political point. I have worked constructively with colleagues in other parties and in other political institutions to call for a national screening programme. For example, I joined the Labour peer Lord Kevin Brennan to raise awareness of some of the symptoms of prostate cancer. We both shared our different prostate cancer journeys, and we discussed why we believe a national screening programme should be introduced. But whether you agree or disagree with a national screening programme, there is clearly a shared understanding across political parties that more can and should be done when it comes to prostate cancer, so I hope that this spirit of co-operation will continue as this strategy is developed.

Now, a key section of the Welsh Government's national cancer strategy consultation considers the opportunities presented by advances in medical technology. We are witnessing significant developments in diagnostic tools and various innovative treatments, many of which are transforming outcomes for patients, including focal therapy, stereotactic ablative radiotherapy and many other treatments. These technological developments can have huge potential, not only to improve survival rates, but also to enhance quality of life for those living with prostate cancer. These technologies must be available to men in all parts of Wales, irrespective of where they live, and I hope the new strategy will show how patients are able to access these specific treatments. Of course, alongside investment in technology, there must also be a commitment to supporting the workforce and ensuring that healthcare professionals have the capacity, training and resources they need to deliver these treatments effectively.

Llywydd, the forthcoming national cancer strategy presents an important opportunity to improve cancer outcomes across Wales, but to achieve that goal, there must be a meaningful consultation process, a commitment to earlier diagnosis and screening, investment in cutting-edge technologies and a determination to provide equitable access to the care and treatment that patients need wherever they live in Wales. We have a responsibility to the men already living with prostate cancer in Wales and to those that will be diagnosed with prostate cancer to use this opportunity to get this strategy right.

And as for a national screening programme, Wales can lead the way if it wants to. We don't have to follow England, we don't have to follow other parts of the UK. So, I urge the Welsh Government to commit to exploring this further at the very least. We all want to deliver better outcomes for men diagnosed with prostate cancer across Wales, and so we will be supporting this motion this afternoon, and I urge Members to support my amendment.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch, Lywydd. Rwy'n cynnig y gwelliant a gyflwynwyd yn fy enw i. Fel y mae'r Aelodau'n ymwybodol eisoes, rwy'n byw gyda chanser y prostad ac fel y cyfryw, rwy'n credu bod y profiad hwnnw wedi rhoi cipolwg go iawn i mi ar yr heriau sy'n wynebu cleifion, a'u teuluoedd yn wir, ledled Cymru. Fel y dywedwyd eisoes, rwy'n un o fwy na 2,500 o ddynion sy'n cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad bob blwyddyn yma yng Nghymru ac fel y clywsom eisoes, mae tua 640 o ddynion yn marw ohono.

Oherwydd y nifer uchel o ddynion yng Nghymru sy'n cael diagnosis ohono, rwy'n credu bod yn rhaid ei gynnwys yn strategaeth ganser genedlaethol Cymru. Yn wir, yn y cwestiynau ysgrifenedig a gyflwynais i'r Gweinidog Cabinet, mae'r ymatebion wedi cynnwys camau a fyddai'n cael eu cyflawni trwy gyfrwng y strategaeth ganser genedlaethol, ac felly nid oes gennyf unrhyw reswm dros gredu na fyddai'n llywio rhyw ran o ystyriaeth y Llywodraeth hon yn y dyfodol.

Rhaid imi ddweud fy mod yn croesawu'r ymgynghoriad ar y strategaeth ganser genedlaethol, oherwydd mae'n gyfle da i feddwl ychydig yn fwy arloesol ynglŷn â sut y gellir darparu gwasanaethau yn y dyfodol. Fodd bynnag, rhaid i'r ymgynghoriad hwn fod yn fwy nag ymarfer ticio blychau, ac fel y clywsom mor aml yn y gorffennol, boed yn ymgynghoriad Llywodraeth Cymru neu ymgynghoriad bwrdd iechyd, rhaid i leisiau cleifion gael eu clywed. Mae'n gwbl hanfodol fod yr ymgynghoriad hwn yn ystyrlon, fod y rhai sy'n cyfrannu ato'n hyderus fod eu barn yn cael ei hystyried go iawn, a bod y strategaeth derfynol yn adlewyrchu'r cyflwyniadau a ddaw i law. Felly, rwy'n gobeithio y bydd y Gweinidog Cabinet yn rhoi'r sicrwydd hwnnw i ni heddiw yn ei ymateb i'r ddadl hon.

Nawr, fel y mae ein gwelliant yn dweud yn glir iawn, mae'r Ceidwadwyr Cymreig eisiau gweld rhaglen sgrinio genedlaethol yn cael ei chyflwyno gan Lywodraeth Cymru. Rwy'n credu bod canfod yn gynharach yn gwella canlyniadau cleifion, ac fel y dywed Ymchwil Canser y Prostad, pan fydd canser y prostad yn cael ei ganfod yn gynnar, mae cyfraddau goroesi yn agos at 100 y cant. Ac nid pwynt gwleidyddol yw hwn. Rwyf wedi gweithio'n adeiladol gyda chydweithwyr mewn pleidiau eraill ac mewn sefydliadau gwleidyddol eraill i alw am raglen sgrinio genedlaethol. Er enghraifft, ymunais â'r arglwydd Llafur, yr Arglwydd Kevin Brennan, i godi ymwybyddiaeth o rai o symptomau canser y prostad. Fe wnaeth y ddau ohonom rannu ein gwahanol deithiau canser y prostad, ac fe wnaethom drafod pam ein bod yn credu y dylid cyflwyno rhaglen sgrinio genedlaethol. Ond p'un a ydych chi'n cytuno neu'n anghytuno â rhaglen sgrinio genedlaethol, mae'n amlwg fod cyd-ddealltwriaeth rhwng pleidiau gwleidyddol y gellir ac y dylid gwneud mwy ar ganser y prostad, felly rwy'n gobeithio y bydd yr ysbryd cydweithredol hwn yn parhau wrth ddatblygu'r strategaeth.

Nawr, mae rhan allweddol o ymgynghoriad Llywodraeth Cymru ar strategaeth ganser genedlaethol yn ystyried y cyfleoedd a gyflwynir gan ddatblygiadau mewn technoleg feddygol. Rydym yn gweld datblygiadau sylweddol mewn offer diagnostig ac amrywiol driniaethau arloesol, llawer ohonynt yn trawsnewid canlyniadau i gleifion, gan gynnwys therapi ffocal, radiotherapi abladol stereotactig a llawer o driniaethau eraill. Gall fod potensial enfawr i'r datblygiadau technolegol hyn, nid yn unig i wella cyfraddau goroesi, ond hefyd i wella ansawdd bywyd i'r rhai sy'n byw gyda chanser y prostad. Rhaid i'r technolegau hyn fod ar gael i ddynion ym mhob rhan o Gymru, ble bynnag y maent yn byw, ac rwy'n gobeithio y bydd y strategaeth newydd yn dangos sut y gall cleifion gael mynediad at y triniaethau penodol hyn. Wrth gwrs, ochr yn ochr â buddsoddiad mewn technoleg, rhaid cael ymrwymiad i gefnogi'r gweithlu a sicrhau bod gweithwyr gofal iechyd proffesiynol yn cael y capasiti, yr hyfforddiant a'r adnoddau sydd eu hangen arnynt i ddarparu'r triniaethau hyn yn effeithiol.

Lywydd, mae'r strategaeth ganser genedlaethol sydd ar y ffordd yn cynnig cyfle pwysig i wella canlyniadau canser ledled Cymru, ond er mwyn cyflawni'r nod hwnnw, rhaid cael proses ymgynghori ystyrlon, ymrwymiad i ddiagnosis a sgrinio cynharach, buddsoddiad mewn technolegau blaengar a phenderfyniad i ddarparu mynediad cyfartal at y gofal a'r driniaeth sydd eu hangen ar gleifion ble bynnag y maent yn byw yng Nghymru. Ein cyfrifoldeb i'r dynion sydd eisoes yn byw gyda chanser y prostad yng Nghymru ac i'r rhai a fydd yn cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad yw defnyddio'r cyfle hwn i gael y strategaeth hon yn iawn.

Ac ar raglen sgrinio genedlaethol, gall Cymru arwain y ffordd os yw hi eisiau. Nid oes raid inni ddilyn Lloegr, nid oes raid inni ddilyn rhannau eraill o'r DU. Felly, rwy'n annog Llywodraeth Cymru i ymrwymo i archwilio hyn ymhellach o leiaf. Rydym i gyd eisiau sicrhau canlyniadau gwell i ddynion sydd wedi cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad ledled Cymru, ac felly byddwn yn cefnogi'r cynnig hwn y prynhawn yma, ac rwy'n annog yr Aelodau i gefnogi fy ngwelliant.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I'm grateful for the opportunity to speak on this really important issue today. There's real excitement across the cancer charity sector and the cancer workforce because a long-term cancer strategy is a chance to set a new course for patients in Wales. This is a critical moment for how we want to see cancer outcomes improve over the coming years, and I welcome every opportunity to discuss what the strategy should look like, because we will all know someone who is told that they have cancer in their lifetime, if not ourselves.

Cancer will affect one in two people. The figures for prostate cancer are particularly shocking. Prostate cancer will affect one in eight men. For black men, it's one in four. And for men who have a family history of particular cancers or who carry the BRCA2 gene variant, they face a significantly higher risk. Reducing this inequality and the many other inequalities in cancer diagnosis and care must be a focus of the strategy.

The Welsh Government has set itself an ambitious timetable, aiming to publish the strategy on World Cancer Day next year. That is commendable and shows the urgency that is needed. It will be Wales's first national cancer strategy since 2006. And as chair of the cross-party group on cancer, which everyone here is welcome to join—I've e-mailed some of you separately; you're all welcome—I'm not aware of any plans for the strategy, as it is at the moment, to focus on any site-specific cancers, which the debate tabled today calls for, but with such a tight deadline, the strategy must build on existing groundwork. There are already national optimal pathways shaped by clinical specialists and best practice that set out how people with suspected site-specific cancers, including prostate cancer, should be treated and supported, but too many people are not being served quickly and effectively by these pathways. There's often a backlog for diagnosis and waits for treatment often depend on surgical space and workforce availability. As a result, only one in three people with prostate cancer start treatment within 62 days, when the target is 75 per cent.

The strategy must not be a 'one and done'. Too many quality statements and short-term plans have sat on the shelf after publication. This strategy must be a living thing. It must give every national optimal pathway, including for prostate cancer, the chance to work to its full potential and actively unblock the barriers holding them back. Alongside this, it must improve access to clinical trials, awareness of signs and symptoms and so much more, like data and workforce. All these things are vital.

I'd like to acknowledge the amendment tabled by Paul Davies, and I share the urgency behind it. General screening for all men is still not recommended by the UK National Screening Committee based on the evidence currently available, but that evidence is moving. In May, the committee recommended targeted screening every two years for men aged 45 to 61 who carry the BRCA gene variant and have a family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer, and the UK Government has accepted that. So, I'd like to ask the Minister: when will this be in place in Wales and will the new strategy commit to it?

I also stand with colleagues in calling for research to go further and faster and for more men to know of their family history. For men facing a prostate cancer diagnosis, support and time to make decisions about their care are essential, but time is not always a luxury patients have. The earlier a diagnosis is made, the more treatment options are available. I hope today's discussion can focus our minds on a near future where prostate cancer is diagnosed quickly and early, where innovative treatments are available and where patients can look forward to life after cancer or to live well for decades to come. Diolch yn fawr.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Can I thank the Member for bringing forward this important debate today and also thank Paul Davies for sharing his experience and his insight into such an important subject matter? And as we've heard during this debate already, prostate cancer is the most common cancer amongst men in Wales and far too many families across the country have lost loved ones because a cancer diagnosis came too late. So, Welsh Labour strongly supports this motion and we join calls to include prostate cancer in the national cancer strategy for Wales. We wish to see a strategy that delivers better outcomes, improves support for cancer patients and builds on the progress made under the previous Welsh Labour Government.

In Government, Welsh Labour ensured that record numbers of people got the good news every year that they don't have cancer. We invested tens of millions of pounds in new cancer facilities, diagnostic equipment, treatments, technology and workforce development, and we started construction on the new Velindre Cancer Centre, which is opening next spring. We introduced a £2 million cancer recovery programme to improve how services are delivered, including a specific focus on urological cancers, and we took significant steps to improve cancer screening and early diagnosis. We expanded bowel cancer screening to everyone aged 50 to 74, and increased the sensitivity of the screening test. We also made Wales the first UK nation to introduce human papillomavirus testing as the primary cervical screening test. Furthermore, we announced a new national targeted lung cancer screening programme, and on all of those decisions, Welsh Labour were driven in our determination to deliver better health outcomes for families in Wales.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
We were certainly right to set very, very stretching targets for cancer. Obviously, we didn't meet them on all occasions, but I do not apologise for the stretching targets that we set. And of all of those decisions, as I say, Welsh Labour were driven at all times by the determination to deliver better health outcomes for the people that we served.

Now, that's particularly relevant today. Decisions about screening programmes must always be based on the best available evidence. In this case, we know that the independent UK National Screening Committee does not recommend population-wide screening for prostate cancer. It advises that population-wide screening can cause more harm than good, because of the risks that include false positives and also the risk of providing false reassurances. Instead, they recommend targeted screening for prostate cancer, and, of course, the UK Labour Government has followed that advice.

The UK Labour Government has committed more than £20 million to improve prostate cancer research and treatment, including supporting the Transform trial, which aims to deliver better ways of detecting the disease. That research is particularly important for understanding how screening can better support black men who face a higher risk of developing prostate cancer. So, will the Minister now confirm that he too will follow the science and the Plaid Cymru Government will commit to introducing an evidence-based targeted prostate cancer screening programme in Wales, similar to that which the UK Labour Government has announced for England? If the Minister is unable to make that commitment today, he should set out his reasons in detail and explain why the Welsh Government is taking a decision that is not led by the evidence.

I'd also urge the Minister to ensure that the national cancer strategy is focused squarely on outcomes and real-life improvements for patients, and that it builds on the measures delivered by the Welsh Labour Government. Because what matters is early diagnosis, faster treatment and better chances of survival for cancer patients. The Minister already has our support for the motion today. If he can make those further commitments on the national cancer strategy, and a targeted prostate cancer screening programme, he will have the full backing of Labour Members as he delivers those plans.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Strategaeth canser y prostad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I'm going to address the men of Wales, and first of all, thank you, Llŷr Powell, for tabling this debate. This is one of those debates where we should be able to put politics to one side. Prostate cancer doesn't care who you vote for, where you live or what you do for a living. When somebody is told they've got cancer, they're not thinking about politics, they're thinking about their family, what happens next and whether they're going to be all right.

This issue is personal to me. My grandfather died from kidney failure caused by prostate cancer, and several other men on my mother's side of the family have been affected by it. That's why it matters to me. I'm thinking about my grandfather and about the families across Wales facing those same worries today. I'm also thinking about the men who may have put off speaking to their GP. I'm 61 now, and because of my family background, I've had the prostate-specific antigen test, and, thankfully, the result was reassuring. But many men don't take that step. Some don't want to make a fuss. Some are worried about what they might be told. Others simply think if they feel fine, there cannot be anything wrong. The reality is that prostate cancer does not always give you a warning. That's why awareness matters and why men need to understand their own risk. But awareness on its own isn't enough. When someone does come forward, the NHS has to be there for them. If they need tests, scans or treatment, they shouldn't be left waiting and worrying about what happens next.

For those of us in rural Wales, there can be additional challenges. A hospital appointment can mean a long journey, time away from work and an entire day spent travelling. If you're already anxious about your health, that only adds to the burden. The latest national prostate cancer audit also raises concerns about variation in treatment in Wales. The figures come with important warnings about data quality, but that itself raises a question: how can we be confident that patients are receiving the right treatment if we cannot reliably measure what is happening?

I also want to say a brief word about the Conservative amendment. I understand the case being made, because I'd like to see more men diagnosed earlier too, particularly given my own family's experience. There is important work taking place around targeted screening for men at particularly high risk, and I believe Wales should continue to follow the evidence and medical advice as that develops.

But today's motion is straightforward. We're asking the Welsh Government to ensure that prostate cancer has a clear place within Wales's national cancer strategy. And inclusion in a strategy must mean more than just a mention in a document. It needs clear commitment on earlier diagnosis, timely treatment and fair access across Wales, with progress that patients and families can actually see—not because prostate cancer is more important than any other cancer, but because it affects so many men and families, and deserves sustained attention.

I'd like to thank organisations such as Prostate Cymru, Prostate Cancer UK, Lingen Davies Cancer Support in my own constituency, and Movember, along with the NHS staff and all the other organisations and individuals who work tirelessly to support patients and their families. Llywydd, I can't change what happened to my grandfather, but I'd like to think we can improve things for the men and families who come after us, because behind every diagnosis is a husband, father, grandfather, brother or friend. And what matters to those families isn't which party brought this debate forward; what matters is what we do next and whether we make the difference. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Rwy'n mynd i annerch dynion Cymru, ac yn gyntaf oll, diolch, Llŷr Powell, am gyflwyno'r ddadl hon. Dyma un o'r dadleuon lle dylem allu rhoi gwleidyddiaeth i'r naill ochr. Nid yw canser y prostad yn poeni i bwy rydych chi'n pleidleisio, ble rydych chi'n byw neu beth yw eich gwaith. Pan ddywedir wrth rywun fod ganddynt ganser, nid ydynt yn meddwl am wleidyddiaeth, maent yn meddwl am eu teulu, beth sy'n digwydd nesaf ac a ydynt yn mynd i fod yn iawn.

Mae'r mater hwn yn bersonol i mi. Bu farw fy nhaid o fethiant yr arennau a achoswyd gan ganser y prostad, ac mae sawl dyn arall ar ochr fy mam o'r teulu wedi cael eu heffeithio ganddo. Dyna pam y mae'n bwysig i mi. Rwy'n meddwl am fy nhaid ac am y teuluoedd ledled Cymru sy'n wynebu'r un pryderon heddiw. Ond mae yna lawer o ddynion nad ydynt yn cymryd y cam hwnnw. Mae rhai'n gyndyn i wneud ffws. Mae rhai'n poeni am yr hyn y gallent ei glywed. Dyna pam y mae ymwybyddiaeth yn bwysig a pham y mae angen i ddynion ddeall eu risg eu hunain. Ond nid yw ymwybyddiaeth ar ei ben ei hun yn ddigon. I'r rhai ohonom yng nghefn gwlad Cymru, gall fod heriau ychwanegol. Gall apwyntiad ysbyty olygu taith hir, amser o'r gwaith a threulio diwrnod cyfan yn teithio. Rwyf eisiau dweud gair byr am welliant y Ceidwadwyr hefyd. Rwy'n deall yr achos sy'n cael ei wneud, oherwydd hoffwn innau weld mwy o ddynion yn cael diagnosis yn gynharach hefyd, yn enwedig o ystyried profiad fy nheulu fy hun. Mae gwaith pwysig yn digwydd ar sgrinio wedi'i dargedu ar gyfer dynion sydd â risg arbennig o uchel, ac rwy'n credu y dylai Cymru barhau i ddilyn y dystiolaeth a'r cyngor meddygol wrth i hynny ddatblygu.

Ond mae'r cynnig heddiw yn syml. Rydym yn gofyn i Lywodraeth Cymru sicrhau bod lle clir i ganser y prostad yn strategaeth ganser genedlaethol Cymru. Ac mae'n rhaid i'w gynnwys mewn strategaeth olygu mwy na dim ond cyfeiriad mewn dogfen. Mae angen ymrwymiad clir ar ddiagnosis cynharach, triniaeth amserol a mynediad teg ledled Cymru, gyda chynnydd y gall cleifion a theuluoedd ei weld—nid am fod canser y prostad yn bwysicach nag unrhyw ganser arall, ond am ei fod yn effeithio ar gymaint o ddynion a theuluoedd, ac mae'n haeddu sylw parhaus.

Hoffwn ddiolch i sefydliadau fel Prostate Cymru, Prostate Cancer UK, Cymorth Canser Lingen Davies yn fy etholaeth i, a Tashwedd, ynghyd â staff y GIG a'r holl sefydliadau ac unigolion eraill sy'n gweithio'n ddiflino i gefnogi cleifion a'u teuluoedd. Lywydd, ni allaf newid yr hyn a ddigwyddodd i fy nhaid, ond hoffwn feddwl y gallwn wella pethau i'r dynion a'r teuluoedd a ddaw ar ein holau, oherwydd y tu ôl i bob diagnosis mae gŵr, tad, taid, brawd neu ffrind. A'r hyn sy'n bwysig i'r teuluoedd hynny yw nid pa blaid a gyflwynodd y ddadl hon; yr hyn sy'n bwysig yw beth a wnawn nesaf ac a ydym yn gwneud gwahaniaeth. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I will declare an interest in this debate, because this particular cancer has come knocking at my own door for a loved one of my family.

I would first of all like to thank my colleague, though, Paul Davies MS, for all the brilliant work that he's already done to raise awareness of prostate cancer. By sharing your own experiences, Paul, which was very brave, you've already actively played a part in encouraging more men to come forward for screening. More than 2,500 men are diagnosed with prostate cancer in Wales every year. Around 640 men in Wales die from that disease annually. And the reason I'm speaking up is because what has happened to me and my family, it can happen to anybody.

We shouldn't just stand by and read out numbers any more of how many people have died annually. In my particular case, two years of monitoring—diagnosed two years ago, two years of monitoring—and the condition was going worse and worse during monitoring, to such a degree now that more extensive surgery is required than would have been had this been picked up sooner. Almost 40 per cent of prostate cancer cases are diagnosed at stages 3 or 4. That is not good enough. When the disease is more advanced, the treatment becomes more challenging. These figures should concern everybody sitting here, including you, Cabinet Minister for Health and Care.

Behind every statistic is a man facing the devastating consequences of cancer, prostate cancer being the most common cancer to affect men. Yet it remains one of the cancers where diagnosis too often comes too late. That is why, as has been said many times here today, and I endorse, early detection must be a priority. The Welsh Conservatives firmly believe that a national prostate cancer screening programme could help to identify the disease earlier, improve survival rates, reduce inequality and raise awareness across Wales.

We recognise that screening must be evidence-based and carefully designed. Concerns have rightly been raised about false positive results, unnecessary treatments and the pressure a screening programme could place on NHS capacity. I also understand that there's been a pushback, certainly from our health board, but also the Government, that too much testing can actually identify problems that could lead to more problems. I'm never convinced by that. A raised PSA result does not automatically mean a man has prostate cancer, but an ever-increasing PSA result is very worrying indeed for the family.

Screening can identify some slow-growing cancers that may never cause serious harm. But these challenges should drive us here, as Senedd Members, to develop a far better approach. Advances in diagnostic technology, including MRI and improved testing pathways, offer opportunities to make diagnosis more accurate, and for better treatment decisions when better informed. We should ensure Wales keeps pace with these developments and adopt proven innovation and evidence as it emerges. We should also recognise that a consistent national approach will tackle those very inequalities that have been described today: black men, men with a family history of prostate cancer and men with certain inherited genetic variations. It is fair to say that a very close member of my family has already died with prostate cancer, so why those warnings were not heeded earlier—who knows?

We acknowledge the recommendations of the UK National Screening Committee, including targeted screening for certain men with a confirmed BRCA2 variant and a relevant family history. The Welsh Government must carefully consider these recommendations. However, we also believe Wales should be ambitious. We should work with clinicians, researchers, charities, and patients and their families, to establish the strongest possible screening approach, informed by evidence and designed for the needs of our Welsh men.

We must also ensure that earlier diagnosis is matched by timely access to high-quality treatment, sufficient NHS staffing and the resources needed to meet demand. I will say this here today: patients from north Wales, patients within the Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, should not be going to London for operations. Devolution was always supposed to be about providing those kinds of treatments here in Wales, and I was really shocked to learn that the robotic equipment that was purchased in the Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board was not the right equipment—that is why we're sending people from north Wales to London. And it has to stop now. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Fe wnaf ddatgan buddiant yn y ddadl hon, oherwydd mae'r canser hwn wedi dod i guro ar fy nrws i yn achos rhywun annwyl yn fy nheulu.

Yn gyntaf, hoffwn ddiolch i'm cyd-Aelod, Paul Davies AS, am yr holl waith gwych y mae eisoes wedi'i wneud i godi ymwybyddiaeth o ganser y prostad. Drwy rannu eich profiadau eich hun, Paul, a oedd yn ddewr iawn, rydych chi eisoes wedi chwarae rhan weithredol yn annog mwy o ddynion i fynd i gael eu sgrinio. Mae mwy na 2,500 o ddynion yn cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad yng Nghymru bob blwyddyn. Mae tua 640 o ddynion yng Nghymru yn marw o'r clefyd hwnnw bob blwyddyn. A'r rheswm rwy'n siarad yw oherwydd y gall yr hyn sydd wedi digwydd i mi a fy nheulu ddigwydd i unrhyw un.

Dylem wneud mwy na chicio sodlau a darllen y ffigurau ynglŷn â faint o bobl sydd wedi marw bob blwyddyn. Yn fy achos i, dwy flynedd o fonitro—diagnosis ddwy flynedd yn ôl, dwy flynedd o fonitro—ac roedd y cyflwr yn mynd yn waeth ac yn waeth yn ystod y monitro, i'r fath raddau nawr nes bod angen llawdriniaeth fwy helaeth nag a fyddai wedi bod pe bai hyn wedi'i godi'n gynt. Mae bron i 40 y cant o achosion o ganser y prostad yn cael diagnosis yng nghamau 3 neu 4. Nid yw hynny'n ddigon da. Pan fydd y clefyd yn fwy datblygedig, mae'r driniaeth yn dod yn fwy heriol. Dylai'r ffigurau hyn fod yn destun pryder i bawb sy'n eistedd yma, gan eich cynnwys chi, Weinidog Iechyd a Gofal.

Y tu ôl i bob ystadegyn mae dyn sy'n wynebu canlyniadau dinistriol canser, a chanser y prostad yw'r canser mwyaf cyffredin i effeithio ar ddynion. Eto mae'n parhau i fod yn un o'r canserau lle mae diagnosis yn rhy aml yn dod yn rhy hwyr. Dyna pam y mae'n rhaid i ganfod yn gynnar fod yn flaenoriaeth, fel y dywedwyd sawl gwaith yma heddiw, ac rwy'n cymeradwyo hynny. Mae'r Ceidwadwyr Cymreig yn credu'n gryf y gallai rhaglen sgrinio genedlaethol ar gyfer canser y prostad helpu i ganfod y clefyd yn gynharach, gwella cyfraddau goroesi, lleihau anghydraddoldeb a chodi ymwybyddiaeth ledled Cymru.

Rydym yn cydnabod bod yn rhaid i sgrinio fod yn seiliedig ar dystiolaeth ac wedi'i gynllunio'n ofalus. Codwyd pryderon, yn briodol ddigon, am ganlyniadau positif ffug, triniaethau diangen a'r pwysau y gallai rhaglen sgrinio ei roi ar gapasiti'r GIG. Rwy'n deall hefyd fod yna wthio'n ôl, yn sicr gan ein bwrdd iechyd, ond hefyd gan y Llywodraeth, fod gormod o brofion yn gallu nodi problemau a allai arwain at fwy o broblemau. Nid wyf erioed wedi fy argyhoeddi gan hynny. Nid yw canlyniad PSA uchel yn golygu'n awtomatig fod gan ddyn ganser y prostad, ond mae canlyniad PSA sy'n cynyddu o hyd yn destun pryder mawr i'r teulu.

Gall sgrinio ganfod rhai canserau sy'n tyfu'n araf na fyddant byth o bosibl yn achosi niwed difrifol. Ond dylai'r heriau hyn ein hysgogi ni yma, fel Aelodau'r Senedd, i ddatblygu dull llawer gwell o weithredu. Mae datblygiadau mewn technoleg ddiagnostig, gan gynnwys MRI a llwybrau profi gwell, yn cynnig cyfleoedd i wneud diagnosis yn fwy cywir, ac i wneud penderfyniadau triniaeth gwell pan fydd gennym fwy o wybodaeth. Dylem sicrhau bod Cymru'n cadw i fyny â'r datblygiadau hyn ac yn mabwysiadu arloesedd a thystiolaeth brofedig wrth iddi ddod i'r amlwg. Dylem hefyd gydnabod y bydd dull cenedlaethol cyson yn mynd i'r afael â'r union anghydraddoldebau a ddisgrifiwyd heddiw: dynion duon, dynion â hanes teuluol o ganser y prostad a dynion â rhai amrywiadau genetig etifeddol. Mae'n deg dweud bod aelod agos iawn o fy nheulu eisoes wedi marw gyda chanser y prostad, felly pam na chafodd y rhybuddion hynny eu hystyried yn gynharach—pwy a ŵyr?

Rydym yn cydnabod argymhellion Pwyllgor Sgrinio Cenedlaethol y DU, gan gynnwys sgrinio wedi'i dargedu ar gyfer rhai dynion sydd ag amrywiolyn BRCA2 wedi'i gadarnhau a hanes teuluol perthnasol. Rhaid i Lywodraeth Cymru ystyried yr argymhellion hyn yn ofalus. Fodd bynnag, credwn hefyd y dylai Cymru fod yn uchelgeisiol. Dylem weithio gyda chlinigwyr, ymchwilwyr, elusennau, a chleifion a'u teuluoedd, i sefydlu'r dull sgrinio cryfaf posibl, wedi'i lywio gan dystiolaeth ac wedi'i gynllunio ar gyfer anghenion ein dynion yng Nghymru.

Rhaid inni hefyd sicrhau bod mynediad amserol at driniaeth o ansawdd uchel ar gael law yn llaw â diagnosis cynharach, ynghyd â staff GIG digonol a'r adnoddau sydd eu hangen i ateb y galw. Fe ddywedaf hyn yma heddiw: ni ddylai cleifion o ogledd Cymru, cleifion ym Mwrdd Iechyd Prifysgol Betsi Cadwaladr, fod yn mynd i Lundain ar gyfer llawdriniaethau. Roedd datganoli bob amser i fod i olygu darparu'r mathau hynny o driniaethau yma yng Nghymru, ac roedd yn syndod mawr clywed nad yr offer robotig a brynwyd ym Mwrdd Iechyd Prifysgol Betsi Cadwaladr oedd yr offer cywir—dyna pam ein bod ni'n anfon pobl o ogledd Cymru i Lundain. A rhaid i hynny ddod i ben nawr. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Strategaeth canser y prostad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Every Member here will have met a constituent who has lived with prostate cancer or a family who has lost someone to it. A man who put off seeing the GP because he felt fine. A wife who noticed something was wrong before he did. A son who now gets himself checked because his father was diagnosed too late. These are not abstract cases. They are our neighbours, our friends and, for some of us, our own families.

Prostate cancer does not affect all communities equally. In our most deprived communities, most men, or more men, are now diagnosed at a later stage than at an earlier one, while men in more affluent areas are more often caught early. In practice, that means that a man's postcode can decide whether his cancer is found while it can still be treated.

According to the 'National Prostate Cancer Audit State of the Nation Report 2026', diagnoses in Wales rose by 12 per cent between 2023 and 2024 to around 2,500 men. That is 2,500 men in a single year who heard the words, 'You have cancer', and 2,500 families whose lives changed in that moment. The same audit found that only 54 per cent of men in Wales with high-risk or locally advanced disease received radical treatment, compared with 69 per cent in England. Those are the men whose cancer is the most dangerous, and too many of them do not appear to have received the treatment that could have saved their lives.

At the same time, 11 per cent of men in Wales with low-risk disease received radical treatment that may not have been needed, compared with 7 per cent in England, with all the lasting consequences that that can bring. The audit urges caution about the Welsh figures because of problems with data quality. Think about what that means. We cannot even say with confidence how many men with prostate cancer are being treated in Wales. That should trouble every one of us, and should be put right.

We also know how hard it is for many men to come forward. Too many have grown up believing that talking about their health is a weakness, and prostate cancer often gives no warning in its early stages. Members of the Senedd have spoken with real courage about their personal experiences, and I pay tribute to them, Paul. Our party leader in Scotland has done the same. But we cannot ask men to be brave enough to come forward and then fail to have a clear plan waiting for them when they do.

Men account for 54 per cent of cancer deaths in Wales. That is why Reform Wales has called for a 10-year cancer strategy, investment in modern diagnostics, targeted screening where need is greatest, and a men's health framework for Wales. So, I call on the Government to name prostate cancer in the strategy, with clear and measurable objectives included, to fix the data, so that we know what is happening to men diagnosed with prostate cancer, and to close the gap between our richest and poorest communities, so that no man is diagnosed too late because of where he lives. I urge all Members to support this motion. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Bydd pob Aelod yma wedi cyfarfod ag etholwr sydd wedi byw gyda chanser y prostad neu deulu sydd wedi colli rhywun iddo. Dyn a ohiriodd weld y meddyg teulu oherwydd ei fod yn teimlo'n iawn. Gwraig a sylwodd fod rhywbeth o'i le cyn iddo ef wneud hynny. Mab sydd bellach yn mynd am archwiliadau am fod ei dad wedi cael diagnosis yn rhy hwyr. Nid achosion haniaethol yw'r rhain. Dyma ein cymdogion, ein ffrindiau, ac i rai ohonom, ein teuluoedd ein hunain.

Nid yw canser y prostad yn effeithio ar bob cymuned yn gyfartal. Yn ein cymunedau mwyaf difreintiedig, mae'r rhan fwyaf o ddynion, neu fwy o ddynion, bellach yn cael diagnosis ar gam diweddarach nag ar gam cynharach, tra bod canserau dynion mewn ardaloedd mwy cyfoethog yn cael eu canfod yn gynnar. Yn ymarferol, mae hynny'n golygu y gall cod post dyn benderfynu a yw ei ganser yn cael ei ddarganfod tra gellir ei drin.

Yn ôl adroddiad cenedlaethol yr archwiliad Cyflwr y Genedl 2026 i ganser y prostad, cynyddodd diagnosau yng Nghymru 12 y cant rhwng 2023 a 2024 i oddeutu 2,500 o ddynion. Hynny yw 2,500 o ddynion mewn un flwyddyn a glywodd y geiriau, 'Mae gennych ganser', a 2,500 o deuluoedd y newidiodd eu bywydau yn y foment honno. Canfu'r un archwiliad mai dim ond 54 y cant o ddynion yng Nghymru sydd â chlefyd risg uchel neu glefyd wedi datblygu'n lleol a gafodd driniaeth radical, o'i gymharu â 69 y cant yn Lloegr. Dyna'r dynion sydd â'r canserau mwyaf peryglus, ac mae'n ymddangos bod gormod ohonynt heb gael y driniaeth a allai fod wedi achub eu bywydau.

Ar yr un pryd, cafodd 11 y cant o ddynion yng Nghymru â chlefyd risg isel driniaeth radical nad oedd ei hangen o bosibl, o'i gymharu â 7 y cant yn Lloegr, gyda'r holl ganlyniadau parhaol y gall hynny eu creu. Mae'r archwiliad yn annog gofal ynglŷn â'r ffigurau Cymreig oherwydd problemau gydag ansawdd data. Meddyliwch beth y mae hynny'n ei olygu. Ni allwn ddweud yn hyderus hyd yn oed faint o ddynion â chanser y prostad sy'n cael eu trin yng Nghymru. Dylai hynny beri pryder i bob un ohonom, a dylid ei gywiro.

Fe wyddom hefyd pa mor anodd yw hi i lawer o ddynion fynd at eu meddyg. Mae gormod o bobl wedi tyfu i fyny'n credu bod siarad am eu hiechyd yn wendid, ac yn aml, nid yw canser y prostad yn rhoi unrhyw rybudd yn ei gamau cynnar. Mae Aelodau'r Senedd wedi siarad gyda dewrder gwirioneddol am eu profiadau personol, ac rwy'n talu teyrnged iddynt, Paul. Mae arweinydd ein plaid ni yn yr Alban wedi gwneud yr un peth. Ond ni allwn ofyn i ddynion fod yn ddigon dewr i fynd at eu meddyg a methu cael cynllun clir yn aros amdanynt pan fyddant yn gwneud hynny.

Dynion yw 54 y cant o farwolaethau canser yng Nghymru. Dyna pam y mae Reform Wales wedi galw am strategaeth ganser 10 mlynedd, buddsoddiad mewn diagnosteg fodern, sgrinio wedi'i dargedu lle mae'r angen mwyaf, a fframwaith iechyd dynion i Gymru. Felly, rwy'n galw ar y Llywodraeth i enwi canser y prostad yn y strategaeth, gan gynnwys amcanion clir a mesuradwy, i drwsio'r data fel ein bod yn gwybod beth sy'n digwydd i ddynion sydd wedi cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad, ac i gau'r bwlch rhwng ein cymunedau cyfoethocaf a thlotaf, fel nad oes unrhyw ddyn yn cael diagnosis yn rhy hwyr oherwydd lle mae'n byw. Rwy'n annog pob Aelod i gefnogi'r cynnig hwn. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch am ddod â'r ddadl yma ymlaen heddiw. Fel rydym eisoes wedi'i glywed, mae'r ystadegau ynghylch nifer y dynion sy'n cael eu heffeithio gan y clefyd creulon hwn bob blwyddyn yn peri cryn bryder. Mae'n bwysig cydnabod nad yw ein cymunedau gwledig yn imiwn i'r her hon. Yn wir, fel nodai sawl astudiaeth, gall y baich fod yn arbennig o drwm ar ddynion mewn ardaloedd gwledig, lle gall mynediad at wasanaethau iechyd fod yn fwy heriol. Mae nifer o ffactorau'n cyfrannu at hyn: y pellter y mae'n rhaid i rai dynion ei deithio i gyrraedd meddygfa; y pryderon ynghylch y gostyngiad mewn gwasanaethau meddygon teulu, fel y gwelwn ym Mhowys ar hyn o bryd; a'r diffyg trafnidiaeth gyhoeddus mewn ardaloedd gwledig. Gall y rhwystrau hyn ei gwneud yn anoddach i ddynion gael cyngor meddygol a'r diagnosis cynnar hollbwysig.

Nid heriau ymarferol yn unig sydd angen inni fynd i'r afael â nhw, ychwaith. Yn aml, gall stigma ac amharodrwydd i drafod materion iechyd personol hefyd arwain at oedi. Gwyddom fod rhai dynion mewn cymunedau amaethyddol yn fwy parod i boeni am iechyd a lles eu hanifeiliaid nag am eu hiechyd eu hunain. Mae hynny'n rhywbeth y mae angen inni ei newid. Rhaid meithrin diwylliant lle gall dynion deimlo'n gyfforddus i siarad am eu hiechyd a bod yn barod i ofyn am gyngor pan fydd rhywbeth yn peri pryder iddynt.

Mae nifer o fudiadau eisoes yn gwneud gwaith gwerthfawr iawn i fynd i'r afael â'r stigma hwn. Mae gwaith diweddar elusen FCN, ar y cyd â Macmillan, i dynnu sylw at yr heriau o ran mynediad at wasanaethau canser mewn ardaloedd gwledig yn enghraifft bwysig o hynny. Yn yr un modd, roeddwn yn falch iawn o weld Undeb Amaethwyr Cymru yn mabwysiadu Prostate Cymru fel elusen llywydd yr undeb eleni. Gobeithiaf yn fawr bydd y bartneriaeth hon yn helpu i gyrraedd mwy o ddynion yn ein cymunedau ffermio a phwysleisio pwysigrwydd adnabod symptomau posibl a chanfod cyngor meddygol yn brydlon.

Er mwyn sicrhau newid gwirioneddol, mae'n hanfodol bod unrhyw strategaeth i wella ymwybyddiaeth a mynediad at ddiagnosis a thriniaeth yn cyd-fynd â chynlluniau ehangach Llywodraeth Cymru i wella gwasanaethau iechyd gwledig. I'r perwyl hwn, rwy'n mawr obeithio y bydd strategaeth o'r fath yn gweithio law yn llaw â dyhead blaengar Llywodraeth Cymru i sefydlu canolfan diagnosis cyflym newydd ym Mhowys.

Mae hwn yn ddatblygiad pwysig i'r rhanbarth. Ar hyn o bryd, mae'n rhaid i rai cleifion deithio y tu allan i Bowys i gael asesiadau arbenigol, gan nad oes gwasanaethau diagnostig priodol ar gael yn lleol. Gall hyn olygu teithiau hir, costau ychwanegol a straen pellach i gleifion a'u teuluoedd ar adeg sydd eisoes yn llawn pryder. Byddai canolfan newydd yn gyfle i wella mynediad at asesiadau amserol, lleihau rhwystrau daearyddol, a helpu i sicrhau bod cleifion yn cael yr ymchwiliadau sydd eu hangen arnynt cyn gynted â phosibl.

Gwyddom fod ymwybyddiaeth a diagnosis cynnar yn hanfodol er mwyn gwella canlyniadau triniaeth ar gyfer canser y prostad. Drwy sicrhau bod anghenion cymunedau gwledig wrth galon unrhyw strategaeth, gallwn wneud gwahaniaeth gwirioneddol i fywydau dynion ledled Cymru. Diolch yn fawr.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Thank you for tabling this debate today. As we've already heard, the statistics regarding the number of men who are impacted by this cruel disease every year cause quite a lot of concern. It's important to recognise that our rural communities are not immune to this challenge. Indeed, as noted in several studies, the burden can be particularly heavy for men in rural areas, where access to health services can be more challenging. A number of factors contribute to this: the distance that some men have to travel to reach a GP; concerns regarding the reduction in GP services, as we currently see in Powys; and the lack of public transport in rural areas. These barriers can all make it more difficult for men to access medical advice and that critical early diagnosis. 

It isn't just the practical challenges that we have to tackle, either. Often, stigma and unwillingness to discuss personal health matters can also lead to delay. We know that some men in farming communities are more prepared to prioritise the health and welfare of their animals over their own. We need to change that. We must foster a culture where men feel comfortable speaking about their health and are willing to ask for advice when something worries them. 

A number of organisations do valuable work in tackling this stigma. Recent work by the FCN charity, in partnership with Macmillan, to draw attention to the challenges in terms of access to cancer services in rural areas is an important example of these efforts. By the same token, I was very pleased to see the FUW adopting Prostate Cymru as the union president’s charity this year. I very much hope that this partnership will help to reach more men in our farming communities and emphasise the importance of identifying potential symptoms and seeking prompt medical advice.

In order to ensure real change, it's vital that any strategy to increase awareness and improve access to diagnosis and treatment aligns with the Welsh Government's broader plans to improve rural health services. To this end, I very much hope that such a strategy will work hand in hand with the Welsh Government's progressive aspiration to establish a new rapid diagnosis centre in Powys.

This is an important development for the region. At present, some patients have to travel outside Powys to receive specialist assessments because there are no suitable diagnostic services available locally. This can mean long journeys, additional costs and further strain for patients and their families at a time already full of worry. A new centre would be an opportunity to improve access to timely assessments and reduce geographical barriers, and it would help to ensure that patients are examined as soon as possible. 

We know that awareness and early diagnosis are vital in order to improve treatment outcomes for prostate cancer. By ensuring that the needs of rural communities are at the heart of any strategy, we can make a genuine difference to men’s lives the length and breadth of Wales. Thank you very much.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Strategaeth canser y prostad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Nothing can ever prepare a person for receiving a cancer diagnosis, or indeed hearing about the diagnosis of a family member or a friend. It's one of the most terrifying things that anyone can be told, and it's a disease that touches, in effect, so many of us. Therefore, I welcome the Government's 10-year cancer strategy, because it's badly needed.

We're hearing today about why prostate cancer deserves proper attention within the national cancer strategy for Wales, and I'll be building on those points. But I also want to share with you a personal experience. I'd like to thank Paul and Janet for sharing their experiences also. My father was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2023. It was the most horrendous news to hear and it's been a very tough experience for our family, especially, at one point, we had an agonising wait of seven days to find out whether or not it had actually spread to his bones. I'm relieved to be able to tell the Siambr today that, three years on, he's still in remission. He doesn't like to have a fuss made of him, and he went through the first few weeks of this process alone because he didn't want to worry anybody. Thankfully, we're beginning to turn the page and move on from a very difficult chapter for us.

Early diagnosis and timely treatment were essential for my father, as they are for all men affected by prostate cancer here in Wales. Ensuring that our health service has the ability and the bandwidth to test and treat the thousands of people in Wales being diagnosed annually is crucial. The 'National Prostate Cancer Audit State of the Nation Report 2026' recorded around 2,700 prostate cancer diagnoses in Wales in 2024, as we've heard, and it increased 12 per cent on the previous year. And as we've heard a few times, but it does bear emphasis, just 54 per cent of men in Wales with high-risk or locally advanced prostate cancer received radical treatment, compared with 69 per cent in England. Meanwhile, 11 per cent of men in Wales with low-risk disease received radical treatment, with concerns that this may represent over-treatment, compared with the 7 per cent in England.

These figures raise serious questions about whether patients are consistently receiving the right treatment at the right time. However, the audit itself warns that problems with Welsh data quality and completeness mean that these findings must be interpreted with caution. Reliable data, modern systems and effective accountability are needed to deliver on its commitments. How can the Government properly assess performance, allocate resources or establish whether its policies are working if it cannot reliably measure what is happening? Cancer services need reliable systems that allow clinicians to access accurate information, co-ordinate treatment and identify delays. The Government must explain how it will ensure that the new platform delivers and how it will hold those responsible to account if it does not.

Llywydd, there is a wider lesson here about funding. In its evidence to the Senedd's Public Accounts and Public Administration Committee, the Wales Cancer Alliance argued that increased investment in cancer services has not translated into proportional improvements in performance or patient outcomes. It also highlighted that the national target requiring 75 per cent of patients to begin treatment within 62 days of their first suspicion of cancer has not been met across Wales as a whole, or by any individual health board, since August 2020. Let us consider that. Years of missed targets across every health board in Wales. That should concern every Member of this Senedd.

Of course, cancer services need adequate funding so that the NHS can afford modern diagnostic equipment, effective treatments, reliable digital infrastructure and properly staffed services. They all require investment. But we cannot simply assume that spending more money will automatically produce better outcomes. We need clear lines of responsibility, transparent performance measures and accountability when commitments are repeatedly missed. Prostate cancer must be included in the national strategy and that must mean measurable commitments on earlier diagnosis, timely treatment, reliable data and reducing unwarranted variation between health boards. And it must mean publishing progress, identifying failures and directing resources where they will make the greatest difference to patients. We should not accept a situation in which the Government cannot confidently establish what is happening to patients because its data is incomplete. The forthcoming strategy is an opportunity to put these failures right.

The Government must explicitly recognise prostate cancer as a priority and demonstrate how investment, digital transformation and service reform will work together to improve outcomes, because men diagnosed with prostate cancer do not need another promise, they need to know that their health is considered, understood and included. They need a health service that can provide the right treatment, at the right time, and demonstrate that it is getting better. That is what accountability looks like; that is what our motion will deliver. I therefore urge Members to support it. Diolch, Lywydd.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Ni all unrhyw beth byth baratoi rhywun ar gyfer cael diagnosis o ganser, neu glywed am ddiagnosis aelod o'r teulu neu ffrind yn wir. Mae'n un o'r pethau mwyaf dychrynllyd y gellir dweud wrth unrhyw un, ac mae'n glefyd sy'n cyffwrdd â gymaint ohonom. Felly, rwy'n croesawu strategaeth ganser 10 mlynedd y Llywodraeth, oherwydd mae ei hangen yn fawr.

Rydym yn clywed heddiw pam y mae canser y prostad yn haeddu sylw priodol yn strategaeth ganser genedlaethol Cymru, ac fe adeiladaf ar y pwyntiau hynny. Ond rwyf hefyd eisiau rhannu profiad personol gyda chi. Hoffwn ddiolch i Paul a Janet am rannu eu profiadau nhw hefyd. Cafodd fy nhad ddiagnosis o ganser y prostad yn 2023. Dyma'r newyddion mwyaf erchyll i'w glywed ac mae wedi bod yn brofiad anodd iawn i'n teulu, yn enwedig, ar un adeg, pan fu'n rhaid inni aros am saith diwrnod i ddarganfod a oedd wedi lledaenu i'w esgyrn ai peidio. Mae'n rhyddhad gallu dweud wrth y Siambr heddiw, dair blynedd yn ddiweddarach, ei fod yn dal yn rhydd o ganser. Nid yw'n hoff o ffws, ac aeth trwy wythnosau cyntaf y broses hon ar ei ben ei hun am nad oedd eisiau peri gofid i neb. Diolch byth, rydym yn dechrau cefnu ar y cyfnod anodd hwn i ni.

Roedd diagnosis cynnar a thriniaeth amserol yn allweddol i fy nhad, fel y maent i bob dyn yr effeithiwyd arnynt gan ganser y prostad yma yng Nghymru. Mae sicrhau bod gan ein gwasanaeth iechyd allu i brofi a thrin y miloedd o bobl yng Nghymru sy'n cael diagnosis bob blwyddyn yn hanfodol. Cofnododd adroddiad cenedlaethol yr archwiliad Cyflwr y Genedl 2026 i ganser y prostad oddeutu 2,700 o ddiagnosau canser y prostad yng Nghymru yn 2024, fel y clywsom, a chynyddodd 12 y cant o'i gymharu â'r flwyddyn flaenorol. Ac fel y clywsom fwy nag unwaith, ond mae'n werth ei bwysleisio, dim ond 54 y cant o ddynion yng Nghymru â chanser y prostad risg uchel neu wedi datblygu'n lleol a gafodd driniaeth radical, o'i gymharu â 69 y cant yn Lloegr. Yn y cyfamser, cafodd 11 y cant o ddynion yng Nghymru sydd â chlefyd risg isel driniaeth radical, gyda phryderon y gallent fod wedi cael gormod o driniaeth, o'i gymharu â 7 y cant yn Lloegr.

Mae'r ffigurau hyn yn codi cwestiynau difrifol ynglŷn ag a yw cleifion yn cael y driniaeth gywir yn gyson ar yr adeg iawn. Fodd bynnag, mae'r archwiliad ei hun yn rhybuddio bod problemau gydag ansawdd data a pha mor gyflawn yw data yng Nghymru sy'n golygu bod yn rhaid dehongli'r canfyddiadau hyn yn ofalus. Mae angen data dibynadwy, systemau modern ac atebolrwydd effeithiol i gyflawni ei ymrwymiadau. Sut y gall y Llywodraeth asesu perfformiad yn iawn, dyrannu adnoddau neu sefydlu a yw ei pholisïau'n gweithio os nad yw'n gallu mesur yn ddibynadwy beth sy'n digwydd? Mae angen systemau dibynadwy ar wasanaethau canser sy'n caniatáu i glinigwyr gael mynediad at wybodaeth gywir, cydlynu triniaeth a nodi unrhyw oedi. Rhaid i'r Llywodraeth esbonio sut y bydd yn sicrhau bod y platfform newydd yn cyflawni a sut y bydd yn dwyn y rhai sy'n gyfrifol i gyfrif os nad yw'n cyflawni.

Lywydd, mae gwers ehangach yma ynglŷn â chyllid. Yn ei thystiolaeth i Bwyllgor Cyfrifon Cyhoeddus a Gweinyddiaeth Gyhoeddus y Senedd, dadleuodd Cynghrair Canser Cymru nad yw mwy o fuddsoddiad mewn gwasanaethau canser wedi trosi'n welliannau cymesur mewn perfformiad na chanlyniadau cleifion. Nododd hefyd nad yw'r targed cenedlaethol sy'n ei gwneud yn ofynnol i 75 y cant o gleifion ddechrau triniaeth o fewn 62 diwrnod i amheuaeth gyntaf o ganser wedi'i gyrraedd ledled Cymru gyfan, nac mewn unrhyw fwrdd iechyd unigol, ers mis Awst 2020. Gadewch inni ystyried hynny. Blynyddoedd o dargedau wedi'u methu ar draws pob bwrdd iechyd yng Nghymru. Dylai hynny beri pryder i bob Aelod o'r Senedd hon.

Wrth gwrs, mae angen cyllid digonol ar wasanaethau canser fel y gall y GIG fforddio offer diagnostig modern, triniaethau effeithiol, seilwaith digidol dibynadwy a gwasanaethau wedi'u staffio'n briodol. Mae pob un ohonynt yn galw am fuddsoddiad. Ond ni allwn gymryd yn ganiataol y bydd gwario mwy o arian yn awtomatig yn cynhyrchu canlyniadau gwell. Mae angen llinellau cyfrifoldeb clir, mesurau perfformiad tryloyw ac atebolrwydd pan fydd ymrwymiadau'n cael eu methu dro ar ôl tro. Rhaid cynnwys canser y prostad yn y strategaeth genedlaethol a rhaid i hynny olygu ymrwymiadau mesuradwy ar ddiagnosis cynharach, triniaeth amserol, data dibynadwy a lleihau amrywiad diangen rhwng byrddau iechyd. Ac mae'n rhaid iddo olygu cyhoeddi cynnydd, gan nodi methiannau a chyfeirio adnoddau i lle byddant yn gwneud y gwahaniaeth mwyaf i gleifion. Ni ddylem dderbyn sefyllfa lle na all y Llywodraeth sefydlu'n hyderus beth sy'n digwydd i gleifion am fod ei data'n anghyflawn. Mae'r strategaeth sydd ar y ffordd yn gyfle i gywiro'r methiannau hyn.

Rhaid i'r Llywodraeth gydnabod canser y prostad yn benodol fel blaenoriaeth a dangos sut y bydd buddsoddiad, trawsnewid digidol a diwygio gwasanaethau'n gweithio gyda'i gilydd i wella canlyniadau, oherwydd nid addewid arall sydd ei angen ar ddynion sydd wedi cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad, mae angen iddynt wybod bod eu hiechyd yn cael ei ystyried, ei ddeall a'i gynnwys. Mae angen gwasanaeth iechyd arnynt sy'n gallu darparu'r driniaeth iawn, ar yr adeg iawn, a dangos ei fod yn gwella. Dyna yw atebolrwydd; dyna beth fydd ein cynnig yn ei gyflawni. Felly, rwy'n annog yr Aelodau i'w gefnogi. Diolch, Lywydd.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. Dwi'n croesawu'r cyfle i ymateb i'r ddadl yma ac i gydnabod pwysigrwydd canser y prostad i'r nifer fawr o ddynion, teuluoedd a chymunedau ledled Cymru y mae e'n effeithio arnyn nhw. Canser yw prif achos marwolaethau yng Nghymru, ac mae canser y prostad bellach yn un o'r canserau mwyaf cyffredin y mae dynion yn cael diagnosis ohonyn nhw. Mae gormod o ddynion yn dal i wynebu oedi cyn cael diagnosis, triniaeth a gofal, ac mae gormod o deuluoedd yn dal i brofi ansicrwydd a phryder wrth aros am atebion. Mae'n rhaid i ni wneud yn well.

Gaf i fod yn glir? Dwi'n deall y pryderon sydd wedi ysgogi'r ddadl hon. Bydd yr Aelodau'n gwybod bod gwasanaethau canser yng Nghymru yn flaenoriaeth fawr i mi. Ym maes canser, mae'r perfformiad o ran amseroedd aros yn parhau i fod yn is na'r safonau rydyn ni'n eu disgwyl, ac mae hynny'n cynnwys rhannau o'r llwybr wroleg. Er bod staff yr NHS yn parhau i weithio'n ddiflino o dan bwysau sylweddol, dwi ddim yn fodlon efo ble rydyn ni heddiw a dylai neb arall yn y Siambr yma fod yn fodlon chwaith. Mae gwellau canlyniadau a phrofiadau i bawb sy'n cael eu heffeithio gan ganser yn parhau i fod yn flaenoriaeth allweddol i'r Llywodraeth yma.

Dyna'n union pam rydyn ni'n datblygu strategaeth ganser genedlaethol 10 mlynedd newydd, y cyntaf o'i bath ers 2006. Bydd y gwaith hwn yn gosod gweledigaeth strategol, hirdymor a blaenoriaethau cenedlaethol i lywio gwaith cynllunio'r NHS a thrawsnewid gofal canser dros y ddegawd nesaf. Mae'r nod yn syml ond yn arwyddocaol: bod mwy o bobl yn goroesi canser, bod mwy o ganserau yn cael diagnosis yn gynharach, nad yw mynediad at ofal yn dibynnu ar ble mae rhywun yn byw, a bod pobl yn cael cymorth amserol wedi'i bersonoli drwy gydol eu taith canser. Rhaid i'r un nod gael ei wireddu ar gyfer dynion sy'n cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad ag i bawb sy'n cael eu heffeithio gan ganser yng Nghymru.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Thank you, Llywydd. I welcome the opportunity to respond to this debate and to recognise the significance of prostate cancer for the large number of men, families and communities across Wales that it affects. Cancer is the leading cause of death in Wales, and prostate cancer is now one of the most common cancers diagnosed in men. Too many men still face delays in receiving a diagnosis, treatment and care, and too many families continue to experience uncertainty and anxiety whilst waiting for answers. We must do better.

Let me be clear. I understand the concerns that have prompted this debate. Members will be aware that cancer services in Wales are a major priority for me. In the field of cancer, performance regarding waiting times remains below the standards that we expect, and this includes parts of the urology pathway. Although NHS staff continue to work tirelessly under significant pressures, I am not satisfied with the current situation and no-one else in this Chamber should be satisfied either. Improving outcomes and experiences for everyone affected by cancer remains a key priority for this Government.

That is exactly why we are developing a new 10-year cancer strategy, the first of its kind since 2006. This work will set out a long-term strategic vision as well as national priorities to guide NHS planning and the transformation of cancer care over the next decade. Our objective is simple, but significant: that more people survive cancer, that more cancers are diagnosed early, that access to care does not depend on where one lives, and that people receive timely, personalised support throughout their cancer journey. This same objective must be delivered for men diagnosed with prostate cancer, just as it must for everyone affected by cancer in Wales.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Strategaeth canser y prostad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
We intend to publish this strategy on World Cancer Day 2027, alongside a national cancer conference bringing together NHS leaders, clinicians, planners, partners, stakeholders and the third sector to share best practice and explore how our national priorities will be delivered across the next decade. Improving outcomes and experience to match the top quartile in Europe will require sustained effort, long-term commitment and honest recognition of the challenges we face. It's an ambition worthy of the people of Wales.

Cancer doesn't discriminate, and nor should we. Our intention is to support improvements across all cancer types and for people of all ages, backgrounds and communities. Importantly, the strategy will cover the entire cancer pathway, from prevention and screening through to diagnosis, treatment, recovery, survivorship and living well with and beyond cancer. The strategy will address the key challenges facing cancer services, while putting in place the enablers needed to deliver sustained improvement. That means looking at workforce, leadership, research, innovation, digital systems, infrastructure and service design alongside the quality and effectiveness of care itself. We also want to accelerate the adoption of new validated tests, technologies and recommended treatments, while strengthening accountability and transparency to drive improvement across Wales.

The strategy is being informed by one of the most extensive engagement exercises undertaken in cancer policy in Wales. A national call for evidence is currently gathering insights from stakeholders and the public, and I encourage all those with an interest in cancer services to contribute by the 31 October deadline. Alongside this, we are undertaking structured engagement with NHS organisations, professional bodies, key partners and the Wales Cancer Alliance.

To Paul's point on consultation, we are listening directly to people affected by cancer through patient engagement forums across Wales, co-ordinated by the Wales Cancer Alliance, to ensure that lived experience helps shape the priorities and actions needed to improve outcomes and experiences for the future. It's important that this process is allowed to conclude before decisions are taken on the final content of the strategy. The programme of engagement is still under way and the final priorities should be shaped by the views, expertise and lived experiences that we are gathering, rather than by predetermined conclusions.

The challenges facing the urology cancer pathway are not unique, but they bring into sharp focus the changes we must make if we are to improve cancer outcomes in Wales. These ambitions sit at the heart of the strategy. While the Welsh Government doesn't directly fund individual diagnostic tests, the strategy will set out how the NHS and its partners will work together to evaluate and introduce new diagnostic investigations for suspected cancer, including for prostate cancer.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Rydym yn bwriadu cyhoeddi'r strategaeth hon ar Ddiwrnod Canser y Byd 2027, ochr yn ochr â chynhadledd ganser genedlaethol sy'n dod ag arweinwyr y GIG, clinigwyr, cynllunwyr, partneriaid, rhanddeiliaid a'r trydydd sector ynghyd i rannu arferion gorau ac archwilio sut y bydd ein blaenoriaethau cenedlaethol yn cael eu cyflawni dros y degawd nesaf. Bydd gwella canlyniadau a phrofiad i gyd-fynd â'r chwartel uchaf yn Ewrop yn galw am ymdrech barhaus, ymrwymiad hirdymor a chydnabyddiaeth onest o'r heriau sy'n ein hwynebu. Mae'n uchelgais sy'n deilwng o bobl Cymru.

Nid yw canser yn gwahaniaethu, ac ni ddylem ninnau chwaith. Ein bwriad yw cefnogi gwelliannau ar draws pob math o ganser ac ar gyfer pobl o bob oedran, cefndir a chymuned. Yn bwysig, bydd y strategaeth yn cwmpasu'r llwybr canser cyfan, o atal a sgrinio hyd at ddiagnosis, triniaeth, adferiad, goroesi a byw'n dda gyda chanser a thu hwnt. Bydd y strategaeth yn mynd i'r afael â'r heriau allweddol sy'n wynebu gwasanaethau canser, gan roi'r galluogwyr sydd eu hangen ar waith i gyflawni gwelliant parhaus. Mae hynny'n golygu edrych ar weithlu, arweinyddiaeth, ymchwil, arloesedd, systemau digidol, seilwaith a llunio gwasanaethau ochr yn ochr ag ansawdd ac effeithiolrwydd gofal ei hun. Rydym hefyd am gyflymu'r broses o fabwysiadu profion, technolegau a thriniaethau newydd a ddilyswyd a rhai a argymhellir, gan gryfhau atebolrwydd a thryloywder i ysgogi gwelliant ledled Cymru.

Caiff y strategaeth ei llywio gan un o'r ymarferion ymgysylltu mwyaf helaeth a gynhaliwyd ym maes polisi canser yng Nghymru. Ar hyn o bryd mae galwad genedlaethol am dystiolaeth yn casglu sylwadau gan randdeiliaid a'r cyhoedd, ac rwy'n annog pawb sydd â diddordeb mewn gwasanaethau canser i gyfrannu erbyn y dyddiad cau ar 31 Hydref. Ochr yn ochr â hyn, rydym yn ymgysylltu'n strwythuredig â sefydliadau'r GIG, cyrff proffesiynol, partneriaid allweddol a Chynghrair Canser Cymru.

Ar bwynt Paul ynghylch ymgynghori, rydym yn gwrando'n uniongyrchol ar bobl yr effeithir arnynt gan ganser drwy fforymau ymgysylltu â chleifion ledled Cymru, a gydlynir gan Gynghrair Canser Cymru, i sicrhau bod profiad bywyd yn helpu i siapio'r blaenoriaethau a'r camau gweithredu sydd eu hangen i wella canlyniadau a phrofiadau ar gyfer y dyfodol. Mae'n bwysig fod y broses hon yn cael ei gadael i orffen cyn y gwneir penderfyniadau ar gynnwys terfynol y strategaeth. Mae'r rhaglen ymgysylltu'n dal i fynd rhagddi a dylai'r blaenoriaethau terfynol gael eu siapio gan y safbwyntiau, yr arbenigedd a'r profiadau bywyd yr ydym yn eu casglu, yn hytrach na chasgliadau y daethpwyd iddynt ymlaen llaw.

Nid yw'r heriau sy'n wynebu'r llwybr canser wrolegol yn unigryw, ond maent yn rhoi ffocws clir i'r newidiadau sy'n rhaid inni eu gwneud os ydym am wella canlyniadau canser yng Nghymru. Mae'r uchelgeisiau hyn yn ganolog i'r strategaeth. Er nad yw Llywodraeth Cymru yn ariannu profion diagnostig unigol yn uniongyrchol, bydd y strategaeth yn nodi sut y bydd y GIG a'i bartneriaid yn gweithio gyda'i gilydd i werthuso a chyflwyno archwiliadau diagnostig newydd lle ceir amheuaeth o ganser, gan gynnwys ar gyfer canser y prostad.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Strategaeth canser y prostad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Dwi'n cydnabod y pryder y mae canser y prostad yn achosi i ddynion a'u teuluoedd a pham y byddai llawer yn croesawu sgrinio. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn dilyn cyngor Pwyllgor Sgrinio Cenedlaethol y Deyrnas Gyfunol ac, ar hyn o bryd, dyw'r pwyllgor ddim yn argymell sgrinio poblogaeth ar gyfer canser y prostad. Er hynny, mae wedi argymell sgrinio wedi ei dargedu ar gyfer dynion rhwng 45 a 61 oed gyda'r gennyn BRCA2 a hanes teuluol gradd gyntaf o ganser y fron, yr ofari, y pancreas neu'r prostad. Rydyn ni wedi gofyn i Iechyd Cyhoeddus Cymru i ystyried sut y gallai hyn gael ei gyflawni yng Nghymru.

Mae'n arfer clinigol sefydledig eisoes i gleifion â chanser prostad lleol risg isel gael cynnig gwyliadwriaeth weithredol, ac rydyn ni'n monitro cyfraddau triniaeth radical drwy archwiliad cenedlaethol canser y prostad, i gefnogi gwelliannau mewn gofal. Mae meddygon teulu yn cefnogi gwneud penderfyniadau a rennir gydag unrhyw ddyn sy'n pryderu am ei risg o ddatblygu canser y prostad. Mi fyddwn ni'n gweithio gyda'r NHS i ystyried a oes angen canllawiau ychwanegol i gefnogi meddygon teulu i gynnal y trafodaethau hyn.

Dwi am roi sicrwydd i'r Aelodau nad ydyn ni'n aros i'r strategaeth i wella'r data canser. Gan weithio gyda sefydliadau'r NHS, rydyn ni eisoes yn cryfhau argaeledd, ansawdd a defnydd o'r data i osod amodau llwyddiant ar gyfer pan fydd y strategaeth yn cael ei chyhoeddi. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi gweithredu a bydd yn parhau i weithredu ar ganfyddiadau adroddiad Archwilio Cymru, gyda cham nesaf y gwaith hwn yn cael ei yrru gan y strategaeth.

Lywydd, mae pawb yn y Siambr yn rhannu'r un amcan eang: canlyniadau gwell, profiadau gwell a gwasanaethau gwell i bobl sy'n cael eu heffeithio gan ganser yng Nghymru. Mae'r strategaeth ganser genedlaethol yn darparu cyfle unwaith mewn cenhedlaeth i sicrhau'r gwelliant hwnnw, nid yn unig i ddynion sydd wedi cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad, ond i bawb y mae canser yn effeithio arnyn nhw yng Nghymru. Dyna'r ymrwymiad sy'n gyrru'r gwaith yma, a dwi'n edrych ymlaen at barhau â'r daith honno gyda chleifion, clinigwyr, elusennau ac Aelodau ar draws y Siambr hon. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
I recognise the anxiety that prostate cancer causes men and their families and why many would welcome screening. The Welsh Government follows the advice of the UK National Screening Committee and, at present, the committee does not recommend population screening for prostate cancer. However, it has recommended targeted screening for men between the ages of 45 and 61 who carry the BRCA2 gene and have a first-degree family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer. We have asked Public Health Wales to consider how this could be implemented in Wales.

It is already established clinical practice to offer active surveillance to patients with low-risk, localised prostate cancer, and we are monitoring rates of radical treatment through the national prostate cancer audit, to support improvements in care. GPs support shared decision-making with any man who is concerned about his risk of developing prostate cancer. We will work with the NHS to consider whether additional guidance is needed to support GPs in conducting these discussions.

I want to reassure Members that we are not waiting for the strategy to improve cancer data. Working with NHS organisations, we are already strengthening the availability, quality and use of data to lay the groundwork for success once the strategy is published. The Welsh Government has taken action and will continue to take action on the findings of the Audit Wales report, with the next phase of this work being driven by the strategy.

Llywydd, everyone in this Chamber shares the same broad objective: better outcomes, better experiences and better services for people affected by cancer in Wales. The national cancer strategy provides a once-in-a-generation opportunity to secure that improvement, not only for men diagnosed with prostate cancer, but for everyone affected by cancer in Wales. That is the commitment driving this work, and I look forward to continuing that journey alongside patients, clinicians, charities and Members from across this Chamber. Thank you.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Llywydd. Can I just start by thanking all Members who've contributed to this debate, and also the Members who haven't contributed, but have actually sat through and listened to the debate? Because I think it's very nice that we've got a debate that galvanises the whole Chamber together. With all of the rumpus conversations that we have in here, it is quite nice to have some that do bring us together.

Ben opened the debate and, as you said, it's the most common cause of cancer in men: 2,500 people diagnosed and, as many people, like yourself, said, 640 of those sadly passing away—sadly too young, a lot of them as well, because the diagnosis wasn't caught early. And that only 54 per cent of men in Wales are accessing rapid treatment compared to 69 per cent in England, and that's something that should concern us all. I know the Cabinet Secretary highlighted—I'll come on to it later—about wanting to be the best in Europe, and I share that ambition, I'm sure we all do, but we need to put a laser focus on this area of cancer, because it is preventable if it is caught early enough.

You also raised the issue, as a lot of Members did, around data. It's something that a number of us who've been here a long time have always heard about cancer care, that the data just isn't there to inform decision making, so having more accurate data is very, very important. You also raised early screening. I know a number of Members raised that and that's something that's also very important. I know Prostate Cymru, for example, have gone out doing screening themselves on top of what the NHS is doing, and I think they've done an absolutely phenomenal job in finding a number of people across the country. Sometimes, those are men, as Members have talked about, who wouldn't naturally go and see a doctor, but they've had the sessions in rugby clubs, in gyms, for example, or down the local pub. So, it's actually been really good that they've rolled that out.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch, Lywydd. A gaf i ddechrau trwy ddiolch i'r holl Aelodau sydd wedi cyfrannu at y ddadl hon, a hefyd i'r Aelodau nad ydynt wedi cyfrannu, ond sydd wedi eistedd i wrando ar y ddadl? Oherwydd rwy'n credu ei bod yn braf iawn fod gennym ni ddadl sy'n uno'r Siambr gyfan gyda'i gilydd. Gyda'r holl sgyrsiau llawn twrw a gawn yma, mae'n eithaf braf cael rhai sy'n dod â ni at ein gilydd.

Agorodd Ben y ddadl ac fel y dywedoch chi, dyma'r achos mwyaf cyffredin o ganser mewn dynion: 2,500 o bobl wedi cael diagnosis ac fel y dywedodd llawer o bobl, yn eich cynnwys chi, fe fu farw 640 o'r rheini—llawer ohonynt yn rhy ifanc, am na chafwyd diagnosis yn gynnar. Ac mai dim ond 54 y cant o ddynion yng Nghymru sy'n cael triniaeth gyflym o'i gymharu â 69 y cant yn Lloegr, ac mae hynny'n rhywbeth a ddylai beri pryder i bawb ohonom. Rwy'n gwybod bod Ysgrifennydd y Cabinet wedi nodi awydd—fe ddof ato yn nes ymlaen—i fod y gorau yn Ewrop, ac rwy'n rhannu'r uchelgais hwnnw, fel pawb ohonom rwy'n siŵr, ond mae angen inni roi ffocws manwl iawn ar y maes canser hwn, oherwydd mae'n bosibl ei atal os caiff ei ddal yn ddigon cynnar.

Fe wnaethoch chi hefyd godi mater data, fel y gwnaeth llawer o'r Aelodau. Mae'n rhywbeth y mae nifer ohonom sydd wedi bod yma ers amser maith bob amser wedi ei glywed am ofal canser, nad yw'r data yno i lywio'r broses o wneud penderfyniadau, felly mae cael data mwy cywir yn bwysig tu hwnt. Fe wnaethoch chi hefyd godi sgrinio cynnar. Rwy'n gwybod bod nifer o'r Aelodau wedi codi hynny ac mae hynny'n rhywbeth sy'n bwysig iawn hefyd. Rwy'n gwybod bod Prostate Cymru, er enghraifft, wedi mynd allan i wneud y sgrinio eu hunain ar ben yr hyn y mae'r GIG yn ei wneud, ac rwy'n credu eu bod wedi gwneud gwaith hollol anhygoel yn dod o hyd i nifer o bobl ledled y wlad. Fel y mae'r Aelodau wedi dweud, weithiau mae'r rheini'n ddynion na fyddent yn naturiol yn mynd i weld meddyg, ond maent wedi cynnal y sesiynau mewn clybiau rygbi, mewn campfeydd, er enghraifft, neu yn y dafarn leol. Felly, mae wedi bod yn dda iawn eu bod nhw wedi gwneud hynny
